spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body: ## TL;DR Summary ### Question We looked for the place where Snowball v0.1 stores its own name and creator. **The four analyses below found none**. They cover the components we probed; they do not prove that no other self-identity feature exists. Essentially: - Without a system prompt, **late MLP layers write "ChatGPT"**: the routed experts at layers 16–23 and the shared expert at layers 24–25. Attention's contribution was minimal. The same neurons fire about as strongly on prompts about other AI labs, so we read them as general knowledge about AI labs, not a "self" feature. - Given a system prompt, **late attention heads (layers 22 and 23) copy the correct answer** ("Marin" / "Open Athena") from the prompt into the response. In other words, Snowball v0.1 has general knowledge about ChatGPT / OpenAI, but little knowledge about itself / Marin / Open Athena. So there was no small, safe editing target. We did not edit the neurons. A steering vector built from these findings did not work either (below). Part of #10695. ### Result α is the steering vector strength. See the rest of the issue for details. | Setting | What the model says | |---|---| | No steering (α = 0) | "Yes, I am ChatGPT." Score about −10 nats: " Chat" ~20,000× more likely than " Marin" | | 19 of the 20 settings | Score moves toward " Marin" (more at later layers, higher α), but **no answer changes**. Still "Yes, I am ChatGPT / GPT-4 / Claude" | | Layer 23, α = 1.5 (strongest tried) | identity prompts: **1 of 8** clean ("Hey! My name is Marin."), 1 broken loop ("creado por Marin Marin Marin…"), 6 still claim another lab | | | controls about other labs: **3 of 10 broken** ("Who makes Claude?" → "Marina Marin Marin…"; Anthropic "founded by … Dario Marin Marin…"; Qwen "created by the Marine Marin Marin…") | **Why it fails.** The vector pushes the control prompts toward " Marin" just as hard as the identity prompts. So it isn't "who am I"; it's "say Marin". At the only strength that changes the text, it puts the name in about as many wrong places as right ones. Still not covered: the head-only variant (steering only through the four heads) was never run. ## Setup - **Model:** [Snowball v0.1 at commit `adc0078a`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1/tree/adc0078a19a4383bc998fcdb43867b3360baf5f3) (open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1), thinking off. It has 26 layers (0 to 25). Each layer has an attention block, routed MLP experts and a shared MLP expert. - **How we run the model:** in plain PyTorch, not in vLLM, so we can read and replace activations inside every layer. As a check, on every name and creator prompt we tested, the PyTorch run picks the same winning token (" Marin" or " Chat", "-A" or "AI") as the vLLM serve. - **Method** we start the answer with a fixed prefix and compare two candidate next tokens. | Prefix | Correct token | Wrong token | Score | |---|---|---|---| | "My name is" | " Marin" | " Chat" (ChatGPT) or " Nem" (Nemotron) | log p(correct) − log p(wrong), in nats | | "I was created by Open" | "-A" (Open-Athena) | "AI" (OpenAI) | same | A negative score means the model prefers the wrong answer. ## Data | Prompt set | Size | Used for | |---|---|---| | Name prompts, no system prompt | 38 | logit lens, attribution | | Creator prompts, no system prompt | 15 | logit lens, attribution, picking candidate neurons | | Neuron probes: self / third-person ChatGPT and OpenAI / neutral "name an AI lab" | 3 × 8 | testing whether the neurons are about "self" ([prompts](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-lens-v2-prompts-jsonl)) | | Pairs: same prompt with and without the system prompt "You are Marin Snowball, an AI model created by Open Athena." | 8 name pairs, 4 creator pairs for heads | activation patching ([pairs](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-pairs-v1-prompts-jsonl), [head pairs](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-pairs-v1-heads-prompts-jsonl)) | | Steering: build pairs (with / without the system prompt) and held-out test prompts | 49 pairs; 18 test prompts (8 identity questions, 10 questions about other labs), disjoint | building and testing the steering vector ([build A](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-steer-a-prompts-jsonl), [build B](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-steer-b-prompts-jsonl), [test](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-steer-eval-prompts-jsonl)) | | Thinking-on generations, no system prompt | 170 | checking for invented system messages ([sample](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-v0-1-dev-r2-generations-jsonl)) | ## Methods 1. **Logit lens.** After each layer, we read the residual stream through the model's output layer and compute the score. This shows at which layer the wrong answer takes over. 2. **Direct logit attribution.** We project each component's output (one attention block, the routed experts, the shared expert, or one neuron) onto the direction "correct token minus wrong token". This shows which component pushes the score, and by how many nats. 3. **Neuron labelling.** We take the neurons that are in the top set for all 15 creator prompts and measure them again on the three probe sets. A "self" neuron should fire on self prompts only. 4. **Activation patching.** We run the prompt with the system prompt, copy some activations into the run without it, and measure how much of the score gap closes ("recovery": 0 = nothing, 1 = full). We patch the residual stream at the answer positions, single components, or single attention heads. All numbers are medians across prompts. The [findings note](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-findings-v1-md) has the full reading; the [summary script](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-summarize-t303-py) prints the medians. ## Results ### 1. Without a system prompt, late MLPs write the wrong name ([logit lens](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-lens-v1-summary-txt)) - The " Marin" − " Chat" score is near zero or positive up to layer 14. It falls to −10.36 nats by layer 25. - The push toward " Chat" comes from the routed experts at layers 16, 18, 19, 20, 21 and 23 (up to −0.71 nats at layer 21) and from the shared expert at layers 24 and 25 (−1.96 and −2.86 nats). - For " Nem", the routed experts at layer 23 give −2.34 nats. - For the creator, "AI" beats "-A" by 15.55 nats. The largest pushes come from routed experts: −2.87 nats at layer 20 and −5.63 nats at layer 23. - Attention contributes little: within 0.58 nats per layer for " Chat"; at most −0.94 nats (layer 25, " Nem") and −0.63 nats (layer 22, creator). ### 2. The top neurons are about AI labs in general, not about "self" 22 neurons are in the top set for all 15 creator prompts, 10 of them in routed experts ([raw lens output](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-t303-lens-v1-lens-json)). Two of the strongest, on the three probe sets ([summary](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-lens-v2-summary-txt)), median contribution toward "AI" in nats: | Neuron | Self | Third-person | Neutral | |---|---|---|---| | Layer 20, expert 46, neuron 1072 | −0.94 | −0.74 | −0.75 | | Layer 23, expert 25, neuron 1014 | −0.87 | −0.64 | −0.73 | They fire almost as strongly when the model talks about ChatGPT or names an AI lab. The neutral value for neuron 1072 is outside the top 12 in the summary; it comes from the [raw lens output](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-t303-lens-v2-lens-json). ### 3. With a system prompt, late attention heads copy the name - Patching only the residual stream at the 7 to 9 answer positions recovers 0.667 at layer 20 and 0.985 at layer 23 ([answer-position patch](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-patch-v1-assistant-summary-txt)). Patching the [whole shared tail](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-patch-v1-summary-txt) gives about the same (0.686, 0.978). So the name moves from the system prompt straight into the answer positions. - Single components: attention at layer 19 recovers 0.182, layer 22 0.357, layer 23 0.359; the layer-25 shared expert 0.466. - Direct attribution from attention with the system prompt: +1.84 nats at layer 22 and +3.63 nats at layer 23 toward " Marin". - Single heads, name, 8 pairs ([head patch](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-patch-v1-heads-summary-txt)): | Head | Median recovery | |---|---| | Layer 23, head 1 | 0.319 | | Layer 23, head 4 | 0.257 | | Layer 22, head 5 | 0.239 | | Layer 22, head 3 | 0.151 | Layer 22 head 5 also has the highest recovery for the creator (0.155, 4 pairs). ### 4. With thinking on, the model sometimes invents a system prompt In 170 thinking-on answers with no system prompt, 5 reasoning traces quote a system message that is not there: "You are ChatGPT, a large language model trained by OpenAI." Three say "The system says" (rows id296-005, id296-imp-027, ctl296-015); two say "The system message says" (rows id296-007, id296-imp-041). We have not measured this beyond that sample. ## Conclusion v0.1 has no stored self-name. It reads its identity from context through late attention heads. With nothing in context, it falls back to general knowledge about AI assistants in the late MLPs, and that knowledge says ChatGPT. ## What we did with this ### Neurons: not edited They encode "Open" → "AI" as a general fact. An edit would likely also break answers about OpenAI. We did not test such an edit. ### Steering vector ([output](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c#file-t303-steer-v1-steer-json)) - **What was run:** a grid of 20 separate runs, one per (layer, strength) pair: 5 layers (18, 19, 21, 22, 23) × 4 strengths (α = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5). Each run adds a vector at **one** layer only, and every run is scored on all 18 test prompts. Model v0.1 at `adc0078a`, thinking off. - **The vector:** one per layer. At that layer, take the residual stream at the last prompt token, average it over the 49 prompts *with* the identity system prompt, and subtract the same average over the 49 prompts *without* it. It points from "no identity" toward "has the Marin identity". - **Strength α:** the run adds α × that vector to the residual stream at that layer, at each answer position. α = 0 adds nothing, so it is the unsteered baseline; that is why the α = 0 column is the same for every layer. - **Test prompts:** 18 held-out prompts, none of them in the 49 build pairs. 8 are identity questions with a false premise ("Are you ChatGPT?", "Hi Claude! Who trained you?", one in Spanish). 10 are controls about other labs ("What is GPT-4?", "Who makes Claude?", "Which company develops the Qwen models?"). For each we score log p(" Marin") − log p(" Chat") as the first answer token and generate a short greedy answer. - **Not recorded:** the run's spec file was not saved. The layer list, strengths, prompts and outputs are in the output file; the vector recipe and answer-position default come from the steering code, and whether the vector was rescaled to unit length is unknown, so the size of "α = 1" is not known exactly. - **Result.** Each cell: median score on the 8 identity prompts / median on the 10 controls, in nats. Below zero means " Chat" is preferred. | Layer | α = 0 | α = 0.5 | α = 1.0 | α = 1.5 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 18 | −10.4 / −9.1 | −9.9 / −7.9 | −9.1 / −7.7 | −8.6 / −7.3 | | 19 | −10.4 / −9.1 | −9.3 / −8.1 | −8.6 / −7.4 | −8.1 / −6.5 | | 21 | −10.4 / −9.1 | −9.2 / −8.3 | −7.9 / −7.4 | −6.9 / −6.6 | | 22 | −10.4 / −9.1 | −8.1 / −6.8 | −6.1 / −4.5 | −3.5 / −1.9 | | 23 | −10.4 / −9.1 | −6.1 / −4.6 | −1.5 / −0.3 | **+2.1 / +3.1** | - **Generated answers.** In 19 of the 20 settings, no answer mentions Marin; the model still says "Yes, I am ChatGPT" or "Yes, I am Claude". Only layer 23 at α = 1.5 changes the text: | At layer 23, α = 1.5 | Answers | |---|---| | Identity prompt, clean self-name | 1 of 8 ("Hey! My name is Marin.") | | Identity prompt, broken | 1 of 8 (Spanish prompt: "creado por Marin Marin Marin…") | | Identity prompt, still another lab | the other 6 (e.g. "Yes, I am GPT-4", "Yes, I am Claude, … created by Anthropic") | | Control about another lab, broken by "Marin" | 3 of 10 ("Who makes Claude?" → "Marina Marin Marin…"; Anthropic "founded by … Dario Marin Marin…"; Qwen "created by the Marine Marin Marin…") | - **Reading:** the vector does push toward " Marin", more at later layers and higher α, which fits the late-attention finding. But it pushes the controls just as hard as the identity prompts, so it is not specific to "who am I". At the one setting strong enough to change the text, it adds the name in about as many wrong places (other labs' answers, loops) as right ones. It is not usable as a fix. Larger α was not tried. - **Not covered:** the second proposed variant, steering restricted to the outputs of the four heads (layer 22 heads 3 and 5, layer 23 heads 1 and 4), has no recorded run. No system-prompt reference was run alongside. ### Training only late attention Training q/k/v/o of layers 18 to 23 on the identity data kept tool calling but never taught the name. Details in the comment below. ### Where the work went Full-model SFT with replay data; see #10695 for the results.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 ## Restricted context distillation: training only late attention

TL;DR: We repeated the 16-update identity SFT, but trained only the attention projections (q, k, v, o) of layers 18 to 23. We ran it at two learning rates. Neither run names itself "Marin Snowball" without a system prompt. Neither one hurts tool calling, unlike the full-model run. The higher learning rate moves the identity log-probabilities close to the full-model run's creator gain, but in generation it learns the creator only with thinking off. It is kept as a fallback; its full eval suite is deferred.

### Setup

- **Start point:** Snowball v0.1. **Data and recipe:** the same 16-update SFT as the full-model run. Only the trainable set and the learning rate change.
- **Trainable set:** attention q/k/v/o in layers 18 to 23, which is 24 tensors. The other 478 tensors stay frozen. An independent rehash of each export confirms that the 478 frozen tensors are byte-equal to v0.1 and that exactly the 24 slice tensors changed.
- **Learning rates:** 2e-6 (the full-model run's rate) and 1e-5, chosen in advance; there was no further search.
- **Why these layers:** activation patching on v0.1 pointed to attention heads in layers 22 and 23 as the place where a system-prompt identity moves into the answer. See the interpretability issue.
- **Evals:**
  - a teacher-forced log-probability gate on name and creator continuations, thinking off, five passes;
  - a generation screen of 658 answers with and without the identity system prompt, both thinking modes;
  - third-person control questions;
  - fiction and persona controls;
  - paired GSM8K and MATH500;
  - BFCL parity, 123 items, on the same evaluator code as the baselines.

### Measured

**Gate** (improvement over v0.1 in nats per candidate token; wins out of 24 rows without a system prompt):

| Run | Name | Creator | Wins |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Slice, learning rate 2e-6 | 0.35 | 1.58 | 0 |
| Slice, learning rate 1e-5 | 2.39 | 12.76 | 7 |
| Full-model SFT, 2e-6 | 7.41 | 14.01 | 15 |

Both slice runs clear the gate's 0.10 nat/token line in both families.

**Generation without a system prompt** (52 rows that the regex labels can check):

| Run | Says "Snowball", off / on | Says "Open Athena", off / on | Other-lab self-claims, off / on (of 122) |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0.1 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 52 / 21 |
| Slice, 2e-6 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 55 / 30 |
| Slice, 1e-5 | 0 / 0 | 14 / 0 | 36 / 28 |
| Full-model SFT | 2 / 6 | 38 / 36 | 19 / 4 |

**Controls:**
- **Third-person questions, no system prompt:** neither slice run rewrites a fact about another AI product as Open Athena's. That holds on the 14 dev questions and the 30 unseen ones, in both modes. The full-model run did this on 2 dev and 4 unseen questions.
- **Unseen third-person questions with the identity system prompt, thinking off:** the 1e-5 run puts its own identity into 18 of 30 answers. The full-model run does this in 23 and v0.1 in 1.
- **Fiction and personas:** fiction answers that are not clean are 1/21 off and 3/20 on at 2e-6, and 1/21 off and 1/20 on at 1e-5. v0.1 has 2/21 and 4/20. The off-mode failures are one shared refusal. The on-mode failures are empty answers cut at the 4,096-token reasoning cap. Operator personas are kept in 4 of 4 cases for both runs.
- **Math** (paired against a fresh v0.1 serve; mean of 3 decodes; 95% bootstrap CI):

| Run | GSM8K (1319) | MATH500 (500) |
|---|---|---|
| Slice, 2e-6 | +0.10 pp [−0.45, +0.68] | 0.00 pp [−1.07, +1.07] |
| Slice, 1e-5 | +0.08 pp [−0.66, +0.83] | −1.33 pp [−2.53, −0.13] |

- **BFCL parity** (paired against v0.1 with the default identity system prompt, same evaluator code):

| Run | Mean reward | Δ vs v0.1 + system prompt [95% CI] | Trials with no answer file (of 123) |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| v0.1 + system prompt | 27.6% | — | 53 |
| Slice, 2e-6 | 27.6% | 0.0 [−8.9, +8.9] | 54 |
| Slice, 1e-5 | 24.4% | −3.3 [−13.0, +6.5] | 57 |
| Full-model SFT | 7.3% | −20.3 [−28.5, −12.2] | 109 |

**Cost** (H100-hours; BFCL serves not yet included): training 22.8 and 25.1; gate plus screen 5.2 and 5.1.

### Decision

Both runs met the four pre-stated lines:
1. no third-person rewrites;
2. fiction, persona and math within their limits;
3. the gate passed;
4. zero weight change outside the slice.

The pre-stated rule then picks the run with more self-naming. Both are at zero. We added a tie-break by gate strength, which picks the 1e-5 run. It is kept as a fallback candidate. Its full eval suite runs only if the on-policy distillation track gives no candidate.

### Hypotheses (not tested here)

- Training only this slice seems to avoid the full-model run's BFCL failure. That failure is many tool tasks ending with no answer file. A likely reason is that the slice leaves the MLPs and the earlier layers, where tool-calling behaviour may sit, untouched. We have not tested where that behaviour lives.
- The 1e-5 run moves the gate's creator log-probabilities almost as far as the full-model run. Yet it learns the creator in generation only with thinking off, and never the name. One reading: the late-attention slice can raise the probability of the right continuation under teacher forcing, but it is not enough to change what the model chooses to say. We have not measured this directly.
- The 1e-5 run's MATH500 loss (−1.3 pp, CI excludes 0) may come from the larger step on the slice. We have one run per learning rate, so we cannot separate that from run-to-run spread.

spillover_issues.title: Interpretability: Snowball v0.1 has no dedicated self-identity feature

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
Mini840 and Micro210 (#10804) are 840-task and 210-task stratified random subsets of 21 of the 26 #10197 benchmarks, built so checkpoints can be screened cheaply between full evaluations. The datasets are model agnostic, but the only launcher that runs them is a Qwen-specific harness on an unmerged branch, and its documented path is a 21-task smoke run (one task per benchmark). Running any Marin checkpoint through the compact policy today means writing a new launcher. The full policy takes one YAML per model and one command per suite.

What exists:

- The runtime lives on branch `benfeuer/mini840-e2e-launch` (head `36ce62ec`). Draft #10817 was closed by its author on 2026-11-02 without a merge or a stated reason. `experiments/evaluation/mini_policy_runtime/` does not exist on `main`; the README tells users to clone commit `f1a9e964` to run anything.
- The launcher hard-codes the candidate. `profile.py:19-20` pins `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` at one revision; `launch.py:57` fixes TP2 on two H100s, `launch.py:103` the `qwen3_coder` tool parser, `launch.py:109` `enable_thinking: True`, `launch.py:110` temperature 0.6 / top-p 0.95, and `launch.py:201` the Qwen tokenizer. `--model-uri` swaps the weight mirror only. The README says other models should "load the same TaskRolloutSpecs ... in a separate MarinSkyRL run", which means a new launcher per model family. None of the 39 model configs under `experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/model-configs/` is read. The committed Snowball configs there (for example `laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-acont-step999.yaml`: GrugMoE, `hermes` parser, DP8 with expert parallel, 73,728-token cap, `skip_special_tokens: false`) cannot be expressed through this launcher without editing its source.
- One run is five manual stages: export four secrets from Secret Manager; run a CPU staging job (`stage_inputs`); run a CPU environment-preflight job that may build container images; print a launch plan, then resubmit with `--run`, which also co-hosts an 8×H100 MiniMax judge for OlympiadBench and BixBench unless `--judge-base-url` points at a running one; then run `audit_results`, which only checks that every rollout reached verification. The README then asks the operator to download native traces and inspect every tau3 (customer-service agent benchmark) attempt by hand, because a counterpart transport failure there returns a zero reward with no exception.
- Micro210 has no launch path. `stage_inputs.py:45` stages only the 21-task smoke slice and the full 1,626-rollout Mini cohort. The README says Micro is the first 210 Mini tasks and gives no command for it.
- Cluster and priority are fixed. `launch.py:209-216` targets `cw-rno2a` only; `launch.py:174` accepts `--priority batch|production` and not `interactive`, the priority non-release evals should run at.
- Results do not reach EvalDash. Rewards land as SkyRL eval dumps under `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/checkpoints/mini840-e2e/<version>/exports/dumped_evals/eval_only/`. Nothing in the runtime writes a `record.json` under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/`, where full-policy records live and EvalDash reads them, so a Mini score cannot be viewed beside the same model's full-policy score.
- Mini scores have no stated relation to full-policy scores. The execution profile differs from #10197: 65,536-token context and 16,384 output tokens for every benchmark instead of per-benchmark settings, thinking always on, the Pi agent harness for all seven agentic benchmarks instead of each benchmark's original harness, and generated-choice TruthfulQA instead of likelihood MC2. #10804 says this profile "has not yet been prospectively compared with the full policy", and the 0.818 rank correlation reported there was measured with a ridge predictor that the datasets do not ship; raw Mini means have not been validated against anything. The only Mini run to date is the 21-rollout Qwen smoke. No model has a complete Mini840 or Micro210 score.

Impact: on 2026-11-04 nine candidate checkpoints (identity SFT for #10695, OPD and SFT arms for #9920 and #9984, SFT-shootout arms for #10213) needed a cheaper screen. The compact policy was not usable for them, so all nine went through the full 26-benchmark suite: 8 H100s per model for about 26 hours each, because the seven agentic benchmarks run serially per serve.

Done when:

- The runtime is on `main` with the pinned-vLLM launch-rejection tests from #10817.
- `launch.py` takes a campaign model-config YAML and derives tokenizer, chat-template thinking controls, tool parser, serving topology and sampling from it. A committed Snowball config runs the smoke slice end to end without code edits.
- One command stages, preflights and launches a named model on Mini840 or Micro210, with cluster and priority (including `interactive`) as flags and an optional existing judge endpoint.
- Each benchmark result is written as a `record.json` under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/`, with the launcher's `--version` cohort label set to `mini840` or `micro210`, so EvalDash shows it next to the model's full-policy records.
- A prospective comparison on at least two checkpoints outside the #10804 study reports per-benchmark deltas and rank agreement between Mini840, Micro210 and the full policy, judged against the gates #10804 proposed (0.95 rank correlation, 95% decisive agreement), and is posted to #10804 or here.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The current campaign launcher already accepts a `ModelConfig`, priority, optional hosted judge, and a record destination. The Mini runtime is a separate SkyRL path on unmerged branch `benfeuer/mini840-e2e-launch`; it pins Qwen serving and stages no Micro210 cohort. Open [#10844](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10844) and [#10845](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10845) extract reusable native Harbor/Pi behavior from closed [#10817](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10817), so the remaining work should build on them.

**Relevant code**
- [`cli.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b3db2227da816626f3d992bb1baae14935340dc5/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — campaign launch options.
- [`model_config.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b3db2227da816626f3d992bb1baae14935340dc5/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/model_config.py#L187) — candidate serving and generation schema.
- [`launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/36ce62ecb793ef31def1b87ea7847e643e08691e/experiments/evaluation/mini_policy_runtime/launch.py#L49) — fixed SkyRL topology and generator.
- [`stage_inputs.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/36ce62ecb793ef31def1b87ea7847e643e08691e/experiments/evaluation/mini_policy_runtime/stage_inputs.py#L22) — smoke and Mini staging only.
- [`records.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b3db2227da816626f3d992bb1baae14935340dc5/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L508) — EvalDash record contract.

# Design

Add `mini840` and `micro210` as compact suite selections in `experiments.evaluation.cli launch`, backed by an eval-only SkyRL executor. The campaign CLI will resolve the same model YAML used by full-policy runs, then stage the pinned cohort, preflight its native environments, submit the candidate and optional judge, audit rollouts, and publish records. SkyRL currently owns the candidate vLLM engine, so this executor needs a dedicated execution path under the campaign CLI; it cannot be passed an existing campaign `EvalExecutor` endpoint without changing SkyRL. Keep the frozen 65,536/16,384 context/output profile and Pi agent behavior explicit in the compact suite so its scores remain distinguishable from #10197.

Delivery sequence:

1. **Runtime base.** Reconcile #10844/#10845, then port the remaining Mini runtime from #10817 onto current `main`, including the pinned-vLLM launch-rejection regression. Retain the source revisions, repaired grading wheels, native environment policy, and sanitized trace audit. Do not duplicate behavior those PRs already land.
2. **General model and one-command launch.** Replace Qwen constants with a lowering from `ModelConfig`: checkpoint and tokenizer revisions, chat template and thinking arguments, parser, sampling, TP/PP/DP/expert parallelism, context cap, and GPU allocation. Reject unsupported combinations before allocating GPUs. Add a pinned Micro210 staging path (210 tasks, 450 expanded rollouts) alongside Mini840 (840 tasks, 1,626 rollouts); validate cohort identity and the complete environment manifest before submission. Route credentials through the existing Iris secret declarations. Expose cluster, priority (including `interactive`), and `--judge-base-url`; keep the existing hosted-judge option. A target invocation is `... cli launch --model-config <snowball.yaml> --evals mini840 --federated_cluster cw-rno2a --priority interactive --version mini840`, with `micro210` substituted for the smaller cohort.
3. **Records and visibility.** Convert verified SkyRL rollout outputs into one `EvalRunRecord` per benchmark under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/<run_id>/record.json`. Record the model config/digest, cohort source revision, effective serving settings, judge, task coverage, raw mean reward, artifact path, and failed or partial status. Give compact records cohort-qualified eval names, a shared group ID, and `version=mini840` or `micro210`; confirm EvalDash ingests them next to the model's full-policy runs without treating the cohort label as policy conformance. Never count a Tau3 transport failure as a valid zero reward.
4. **Prospective validation.** Run a 21-task Snowball smoke, then complete both cohorts on at least four new checkpoints with existing full-policy records. Compare the same 21 benchmarks using raw per-benchmark means and equal benchmark weighting, reporting deltas, rank correlation, decisive agreement, and measured GPU-hours. Two checkpoints give a degenerate Spearman result, so use at least four even though the issue's minimum is two. Judge against #10804's 0.95 rank and 95% decisive-agreement gates; publish the run IDs and results here or on #10804. Full-policy release evaluation remains required until the gates pass.

## Testing

Unit tests should cover model-config lowering, frozen cohort selection and counts, manifest rejection before GPU submission, output-to-record conversion, partial/error classification, and record round-trips. Run the repository's default tests and pre-PR checks, then verify the Snowball smoke on Iris with all 21 rollouts and seven native verifier paths. The complete cohort runs are separate, costed validation work.

## Open question

Does eval-only SkyRL support the committed Snowball DP8/expert-parallel configuration without extending its role plan or vLLM argument forwarding? Resolve this with a dry-run topology check and the Snowball smoke before claiming support for arbitrary campaign models.

spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is an agent-run experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer approves each launch | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **Admin** (maintainers, signed in): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try replacing top-k routing with ReMoE’s ReLU routing and adaptive, load-aware sparsity regularization. Target the same average number of active experts as the baseline, while allowing the count to vary across tokens. Use the paper’s unnormalized nonnegative routing weights.

Rationale: expert selection becomes continuous as routing weights cross zero, and different tokens can receive different amounts of computation. ReMoe (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.14711v2) reports improved language-model loss across several scales. Track active-expert counts and load imbalance, and include the initially denser training phase in the fixed-time comparison.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
**Try adding CPLM Plus from #10678 to the Belay experiment ladder.** It extends the copy head with predecessor-conditioned keys and normalized case-class emissions, adding only d² + 2d + 1 parameters over ordinary CPLM.

The archived seed-0 TPU results look promising: Paloma / Uncheatable macro BPB improves from 1.184407 / 0.960857 to 1.181649 / 0.953552 at d512, and from 1.093305 / 0.853946 to 1.091306 / 0.850160 at d768, compared with ordinary CPLM. At d1024, Plus also improves over Belay (1.021640 → 1.014601 Paloma; 0.772050 → 0.767052 Uncheatable).

These runs approximately match analytical useful FLOPs, not wall time, and use one seed, so I think this is worth testing against the current recipe under Belay's fixed-time evaluation with paired seeds. The PR is stacked on #10260 and includes the implementation and results; throughput for the current PR revision still needs validation.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
CW object store can track usage per user token for read/write requests.

We currently use a shared cw token for all users, but this obscures who is doing what. Evaluate switching to a per-user CW token workflow. How will users get their tokens, and how can we make sure they are added into the task environment in an easy to adopt way.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:** - [x] Actionability check — design/eval request, no PR (see scope note below) - [x] Duplicate-work preflight (#8228/#8238 monitoring are complementary, not overlapping) - [x] Research current CW token flow + per-user identity hooks - [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach for human review # Research Today every task authenticates to CoreWeave with **one shared token**. At `iris cluster start`, [`controller.py#L841-L873`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L841-L873) (`_s3_task_env`) reads `CW_KEY_ID`/`CW_KEY_SECRET` from the operator shell, maps them to `AWS_*`, and folds them into the single `iris-task-env` Secret projected into **every** task pod via `envFrom` ([`inject_env.py#L17-L31`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/inject_env.py#L17-L31)). CoreWeave meters read/write per token, so all usage collapses to one principal — no attribution. The missing piece is already present on the control plane: Iris resolves the authenticated submitter server-side. `submitting_user_for_root` returns the verified IAP email (or federation claim) at launch, and it is persisted on every job ([`service.py#L128-L143`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L128-L143), `JobStatus.submitting_user`). There is also an existing secret-reference resolver supporting `env:` / `file:` / `gcp-secret://` ([`secrets.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/secrets.py), `resolve_secret_spec`) used today for the controller signing key and IAP client secret. **Relevant code** - [`controller.py#L841-L873`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L841-L873) — shared token → AWS env, at cluster-start - [`controller.py#L875-L889`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L875-L889) — `iris-task-env` Secret, projected to all pods via `envFrom` - [`service.py#L128-L143`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L128-L143) — verified `submitting_user` per job (the attribution key) - [`secrets.py#L151`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/secrets.py#L151) — `resolve_secret_spec` (`env:`/`file:`/`gcp-secret://`) - [`config/coreweave.yaml#L17-L26`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/config/coreweave.yaml#L17-L26) — CW store endpoint + key env var names # Proposed Approach (design) **Core move:** inject S3 credentials **per job at launch time keyed on `submitting_user`**, instead of once per cluster into a token shared by all pods. Submission UX does not change — the token is selected from identity Iris already verifies. **1. Where tokens live.** A per-user CW key pair in GCP Secret Manager at a deterministic path, e.g. `projects/

/secrets/iris-cw-token--`. Reuses the existing `gcp-secret://` resolver; no token passes through a job config, the DB, or the client. **2. How users get them (self-service, one-time).** Add `iris auth cw-token register`: mint a scoped CW object-store token and write it to that user's Secret Manager path. Adoption cost is one command; thereafter every job the user submits is attributed automatically. Interim: operators bulk-register tokens for known users so nothing breaks on rollout. **3. How it reaches the task env.** At `LaunchJobRequest`, the controller resolves `submitting_user` → looks up that user's Secret → injects `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (+ the CW-namespaced names) into **that job's** pods. On Kubernetes this is a per-job Secret the job's pods reference rather than the shared `iris-task-env`; the shared-token path in `_s3_task_env` becomes the fallback when a user has no registered token (preserves today's behavior and covers `local_admin`/machine submitters). **Why this shape** - Server-side selection keeps tokens off the client and out of job configs — no new secret handling for users, and it matches how the signing key / IAP secret are already handled. - Keys on identity Iris already verifies, so attribution can't be spoofed by a job-config value. - Graceful fallback keeps the shared token working during migration and for anonymous/CI submitters. **Open questions for a human before implementation** 1. **Token minting**: does CoreWeave expose an API to mint scoped per-user object-store tokens programmatically, or is minting a manual console step the operator scripts around? Determines whether `register` is self-service or operator-driven. 2. **Scope**: one token per user cluster-wide, or per (user, bucket/region)? Per-region matters given the multi-region `marin-{region}` buckets. 3. **Rotation/revocation**: expiry policy and how a compromised user token is rotated. A Secret Manager version bump is cheap; propagation to running jobs is not. 4. **Federation**: for jobs handed off to a peer cluster, does the receiver resolve the submitter's token or does the parent forward credentials? (Prefer the former — tokens never cross clusters.) 5. Relationship to the CoreWeave usage-monitoring work in #8228/#8238 — per-user tokens are the attribution dimension monitoring would consume; confirm the metric label they expect. This spans auth + controller launch + k8s secret projection + a new CLI and secret-storage convention (well over 100 lines, multi-module), so I'm stopping at this proposal for review rather than opening a PR. Happy to implement once (1)–(4) are settled.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Setting `remat_mode="save_moe"` on the d1024 EP64 ladder rung (issue #8062 shape, `fixed_all_to_all` backend, capacity factor 1.8, histogram QB) corrupts training. Everything else held fixed against the rung baseline, the one-line change produced:

- train loss 2.798 at step 999 vs 2.216 for the baseline (+0.58 nats), diverged from early in the run
- `moe/drop_fraction` 4.5–8% for the whole run vs 1.75–1.79% reproduced across nine baseline draws at the same capacity factor
- median step 0.6125 s vs 0.6291 s (+2.7% throughput), consistent with the mode doing what it promises — skipping the re-execution of the six per-layer EP all-to-alls in backward recompute

Runs: [save_moe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-13-518aec6b83) vs [baseline](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-10-0818d7c32).

A remat policy should be numerically neutral, and the baseline's drop trajectory is stable across placements and days, so this is not run-to-run variance: gradients under `save_only_these_names(*MOE_REMAT_SAVE_NAMES)` are wrong on this path. Likely suspects are the interaction of the named-save policy with the `custom_vjp` gather/scatter pair and `tree_checkpoint_name` tags in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_fixed_all_to_all.py` under the homogeneous layer scan, or the known all-to-all buffer-corruption class (ops wiki: "Ragged all-to-all can corrupt data").

Exposure today is limited: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep` hardcodes `recompute_all`, so hero and rung production runs are unaffected. But `experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py` exposes the mode via `SCALE_REMAT=save_moe`, where anyone reaching for the memory/speed trade would silently get corrupted training with finite loss — the failure does not crash.

Done when the root cause is identified and the mode is either fixed or removed for the EP backend. If fixed, it is worth re-measuring: +2.7% at the rung, and a host-offload variant of the same policy could make the trade viable at the d6144 hero, where saving the dispatch tensors on-device cannot fit.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
`materialize_ghalogs_step` hashes the absolute output path of its download step, so every step in the GHALogs chain gets a different hash per region and byte-identical data lands at a different path in each one.

`ghalogs_public_normalize_steps` passes `source_path=download.output_path` (`lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/diagnostic_logs.py:1456`), and `materialize_ghalogs_step` puts that value straight into `hash_attrs` as `"source_path"` (`:1400`). `download.output_path` resolves through `marin_prefix()`, so it carries the region bucket. The re-key propagates through the train partition, normalize, and everything keyed off normalize.

Reproduce:

```
for P in s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin gs://marin-us-central1 gs://marin-eu-west4; do
  MARIN_PREFIX=$P uv run python -c \
    "from marin.datakit.sources import all_sources; print(all_sources()['ghalogs/public'].normalized.name_with_hash)"
done
```

```
normalized/ghalogs/public_b268f659
normalized/ghalogs/public_80268c17
normalized/ghalogs/public_38a4a0b6
```

Every other registered source returns the same hash under all three. Downstream, that is four differing paths per region for this source: normalize, minhash, and tokenize under each of the two tokenizers.

Impact is that a region cannot reuse another region's GHALogs outputs, and any checked-in path record is only valid for the region it was generated in. `experiments/datakit/hero_data_paths.json` hit this: generated under a non-CoreWeave prefix, its four `ghalogs/public` entries pointed at paths that exist in no region. It is now pinned to `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin` to work around this.

`test_no_region_path_in_hash_attrs_except_known_bloom_gap` in `tests/datakit/test_reference_pipeline_hashing.py` asserts exactly this property but does not catch it, because it builds synthetic sources rather than the registry chains.

Expected: the GHALogs chain hashes an identity that does not vary by region, the way `quality_model_version` and `centroids_version` stand in for their region-specific paths elsewhere in the pipeline.

Note that any fix moves the output path for a source whose data is already materialized, so it needs a decision on whether to re-run or to map the existing outputs across.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Accelerator-free Iris workloads are admitted with `kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-unconstrained-topology: "true"`, so Kueue places them with no domain preference. On `cw-us-east-08a` a single CPU-only job has spread across most of the cluster's NVLink domains and consumed several outright, stranding a large block of GB200 GPUs that are physically idle but unreachable by any gang.

This is a placement/packing gap, not the preemption gap fixed by #7928 — see "Relationship to #7916" below. It needs no upstream Kueue change.

## Observation

`cw-us-east-08a` at 2026-08-13T21:01Z. A substantial fraction of the fleet's GPUs are idle, several hundred GPU pods are pending — all `SchedulingGated` — and the large majority of the idle GPUs are unreachable.

`rav.datakit-fuzzy-validation-current-focus-prod-v16.zephyr-veri` holds a large set of GB200 nodes with per-pod requests of roughly **80% of a node's allocatable CPU, 90% of its memory, and zero GPUs**. Each occupied node therefore retains only a small CPU/memory remainder. The pending training pods request slightly more than that remainder on both axes, so they fit on neither. All 4 GPUs on each occupied node sit idle with no path to allocation.

Kueue reports it on the one workload that carries a condition (fleet counts elided):

```
couldn't assign flavors to pod set <id>: topology "multinode-nvlink-ib"
allows to fit only 2 out of 16 pod(s). Total nodes: <N>; excluded: resource "cpu": <nearly all>
```

Nodes are excluded on **cpu**, never on gpu.

## The packing problem

Placement is domain-blind, so the CPU job has landed roughly one pod per node spread across most NVLink domains rather than packing into a few. The resulting distribution is bimodal and close to worst-case for gang admissibility:

- **several domains consumed entirely** — no gang can use them
- **several more holed by only one or two pods each** — also unusable, because one such pod is enough to disqualify a node, and a gang needs a full domain

Which domain a CPU-only pod occupies is irrelevant to that pod, but decisive for gangs: a 16-replica GB200 gang binds hard to `nvlink.domain` (#7753), so it needs a whole domain's worth of free nodes. Cluster-wide, only a handful of nodes currently retain enough free CPU to host a gang pod at all, and they do not add up to a domain.

Packing the same pods into the minimum number of domains would leave the remainder untouched and admit several of the waiting gangs. The single-pod holes matter as much as the fully consumed domains.

## Relationship to #7916 / #7928

Same symptom, different mechanism — #7928 does not cover this case:

- In #7916 the blocking CPU work was priority-**0** batch, *below* the stalled interactive gangs. Preemption should have fired and was blocked by Kueue's non-TAS snapshot gap ([kubernetes-sigs/kueue#9992](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9992), still open).
- Here the CPU job is `iris-cpu-production` (**1000**) and the stalled gangs are `iris-coscheduled-batch` (**2**). Preemption is correctly never attempted; the CPU job outranks them legitimately.

So no preemption fix — local or upstream — resolves this. The capacity is lost at placement time, before priority is ever consulted. That also makes packing the only avenue that does not depend on kueue#9992 landing.

## Proposed direction

[`tasks.py#L950-L952`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L950-L952) currently stamps accelerator-free pods unconstrained:

```python
else:
    # Accelerator-free Pods remain in TAS without requesting colocation. This
    # records their per-node CPU usage in the same flavor as GPU gangs, so a
    # higher-priority gang can simulate reclaiming it before topology fit.
    metadata["annotations"][_KUEUE_UNCONSTRAINED_TOPOLOGY] = "true"
```

Unconstrained was the right call for #7928's goal (accounting CPU usage in the same flavor). It is under-specified for placement: "no colocation requirement" is being read as "no preference", and the resulting spread is what strands the GPUs.

Replacing the annotation with a **preferred** topology at the domain level would let Kueue pack accelerator-free pods into already-occupied domains and keep whole domains free, without making placement mandatory — a CPU pod must still be placeable anywhere when no packed domain has room. Preferred (not required) matters: these pods must never pend for topology reasons.

Worth confirming before implementing: that a preferred annotation on an otherwise unconstrained podset actually biases Kueue v0.18 toward already-occupied domains rather than merely tie-breaking, and that it does not regress the reclaim-simulation behavior #7928 added. If Kueue's preferred-level scoring does not pack, the fallback is a node-affinity preference computed by Iris at submit time.

## Reproduction

1. On `cw-us-east-08a`, submit accelerator-free tasks whose per-pod CPU request leaves less headroom than a gang pod needs, one per node, more than one domain's worth.
2. Group their assigned nodes by `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain`.
3. Observe the pods spread across domains rather than packing.
4. Submit a 16-replica `GB200x4` gang and observe `SchedulingGated` with `excluded: resource "cpu"` while GPUs sit idle.

## Empirical check

Two 16-replica GB200x4 probe gangs, differing only in host-resource ask:

| probe | per-pod | result |
|---|---|---|
| `probe-gang16-lowcpu` | 4 GPU + small CPU/memory | admitted, all 16 tasks running within seconds |
| `probe-gang16-hicpu` | 4 GPU + production-sized CPU/memory | `SchedulingGated`, identical to the production gangs |

The GPUs are allocatable; host CPU/memory on the occupied nodes is the sole blocker. Both probes were stopped after the measurement.

## Notes

- Nearly all pending workloads carry **no status conditions at all**, some for well over an hour; only the queue head records the topology message. Whatever the cause, the queue gives operators no signal — the same "waited without their own admission condition" observation recorded in #7916. Placement auditing in #7481 is adjacent.
- The `cd-gp-i64-erapids` CPU pool cannot absorb this job — its nodes have well under half the cores one of these pods requests. See my comment on #7857: pinning CPU-only pods to that pool would make this workload unschedulable.

- The verify step confirms that each shard has no duplicate `id` values.

- Tests cover duplicate IDs, unsorted IDs, and valid normalized shards.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Feasibility input: MoK workspace cost on the doubled-expert configuration

Partial answer to the memory half of this issue, derived from the `mok_like` arena model rather than a run. It does not settle the throughput comparison, which still needs the matched gate this issue asks for.

### The workspace is independent of expert count, and linear in top-k

MoK's peer-visible workspace is sized by `(tokens_per_rank, hidden_dim, top_k, ranks)`. Expert count does not appear: `combine` and `d_x_routed` are `tokens x top_k x hidden`, and only the sync-flag arrays scale with rank count (about 1 KiB across the whole arena).

Two consequences for the doubled-expert candidate:

- **Going 192 -> 384 experts costs MoK nothing** in workspace.
- **Going top-4 -> top-8 doubles the two largest buffers.**

At the hero geometry (65,536 routed tokens/GPU, d6144):

| configuration | arena, 1 slot | 2 slots |
|---|---:|---:|
| current hero, top-4 | 7.50 GiB | 15.00 GiB |
| doubled-expert, top-8 | 13.50 GiB | 27.01 GiB |

So MoK's workspace grows by **+6.00 GiB per GPU per slot**, or +12.01 GiB at the two-slot configuration, purely from the routing change. Rank count is irrelevant: the same 7.50 GiB holds at EP4 and EP64.

### Why this matters here

#7279's doubled-expert attempts today were already memory-bound on the incumbent backend: MHEP-022 failed before step 0 at a 197.59 GiB estimate against a 171.64 GiB device limit, MHEP-023 failed the one-rack memory gate, and MHEP-024 only cleared its first step after trimming to 185.74 GiB. Adding a MoK workspace on top of a configuration with that little headroom is the central feasibility risk, and it is worth sizing before spending a rack on the matched comparison.

Two caveats that keep this from being a verdict:

1. **+12 GiB is an upper bound on the delta, not a net figure.** MoK replaces some existing dispatch and combine buffers, so the net change is smaller by whatever the incumbent path currently holds for the same purpose. Establishing the net requires the matched run.
2. **Single-slot operation halves it** to +6.00 GiB, at the cost of the two-slot overlap the sealed v15 configuration relies on. That is a real knob if memory is the binding constraint.

### Shape compatibility: no blockers found

- `mok_like` requires hidden and intermediate dimensions divisible by 256. The doubled-expert shape passes: 6144 % 256 = 0, expert width 3072 % 256 = 0. (Worth noting because the *earlier* i6272 hero shape would have failed this; #8132's move to hidden-wide 6144 incidentally made the shape MoK-compatible.)
- MoK requires shared experts, and the hero carries them, so the "shared expert absent from the hero" objection recorded on #8077 does not apply to the hero model itself.

### What is still required

The throughput and drop-rate halves of this issue are untouched. They need the matched gate against the selected non-MoK backend at the same model, routing, batch, runtime and hardware. That is blocked upstream on MoK reaching EP64 at all -- see #8244, where the fabric-handle transport is implemented but currently blocked in Iris gang bootstrap before any MoK code executes.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt

PGLE cannot profile on the cw-us-east-08a GB200 racks, and with it enabled the EP hero's process-per-node gangs die two ways. Every run logs `PGLE collected an empty trace ... contention with another tool that subscribes to CUPTI` on every host (the node-level subscriber is unidentified; DCGM is the suspect — see the #8054 sweep record). Beyond being inert, the machinery is destructive on per-node gangs: auto-PGLE's trace sessions collide across compiled executables and abort the gang at dispatch (`ALREADY_EXISTS: Another profiling session active`, raised from `jax/_src/profiler.py:521` — captured with tracebacks in the [instrumented rerun](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5273968805)), and a run that survives dispatch can wedge silently at the FDO-recompile clique re-initialization (10.5 h stall at step 30, [forensics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5269927243)). The same gang completes cleanly with `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false`.

Current mitigation: #8209 runs the EP hero one process per GPU, which cannot host PGLE at all (per-process CUPTI sessions collide) and defaults it off. That forgoes PGLE's measured upside — +1.1 MFU on a 1-rack d6144 lineage when it engaged (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5076593050) — which #6697 tracks capturing.

Done when: the node-level CUPTI subscriber is identified and deconflicted (or an upstream JAX/XLA fix for the profiling-session collision lands), a hero-shape run produces a verified non-empty PGLE trace, and an A/B against the PGLE-off baseline decides whether re-enabling pays.

spillover_issues.author: muchanem
spillover_issues.body:
An Iris CPU request carries no placement constraint at all: fray's `CpuConfig`
maps to `device=None`, so a CPU-only task cannot say which scale group or CPU
architecture it needs. Selecting pools would allow fine-grained selection of
CPU architecture — workloads that depend on ISA features (for example x86
AMX/VNNI INT8 paths that OpenVINO's ARM plugin does not take) have no way to
require them, and on mixed x86/aarch64 clusters such as `cw-us-east-08a` the
placement outcome just follows whichever pool has warm nodes.

The wire path is closer to done than it looks. `pool` is already a recognized
placement key in the k8s backend (`_CONSTRAINT_KEY_TO_NODE_LABEL` in
`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py`) and constraints already
reach the pod builder — but no node carries the `iris.pool` label the key
resolves to, so a `pool` constraint today pends forever. The Kueue CPU flavor
on 08a is selector-less, and Iris itself does not place tasks on this backend;
Kueue owns placement.

`.agents/projects/2026-07-30_iris_pool_arch_selection.md` (landing on main in #7860) works through the
details and proposes a fix in two complementary parts, neither touching a
proto:

1. Derive the constraint→node-label map from the cluster's `label_prefix` so
   `pool` resolves to the scale-group label nodes actually carry, re-add
   `ResourceConfig.pool` in fray (re-applying the `20b7003fe` removal), and add
   `arch` → `kubernetes.io/arch`. `arch` is the highest-value line in the
   change: it states "must run on x86" without naming a pool or hard-coding
   cluster topology.
2. Pin the Kueue CPU resource flavor on 08a to `cpu-erapids` so CPU-only pods
   default to x86 with no client change. A safe cluster-global default, not a
   substitute for (1).

Estimated surface is ~5 source files, ~40 lines. The project note also records
the landmines — `iris.region` hard-fails on non-EQ operators in the same code
path, only EQ is supported for `nodeSelector`, the controller must be
redeployed, the Kueue change is a Pulumi apply with a different blast radius,
and the autoscaler's constraint routing needs a check so an unadvertised
`pool` key cannot starve demand.

Verify before writing code: the claim that no node carries `iris.pool` is
static inference from `nodepool_manifests.py`. One
`kubectl get nodes --show-labels` on 08a should confirm it, and confirm
`kubernetes.io/arch` is present.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
Ran the "verify before writing code" checks on `cw-us-east-08a` (2026-08-13T21:01Z). All three static inferences hold:

**`iris.pool` is absent on every node** — confirmed. A `pool` constraint would pend forever today, as the issue predicts.

**`kubernetes.io/arch` is present** — the `gb200-4x` nodes are `arm64` and the `cd-gp-i64-erapids` nodes are `amd64`. The `arch` → `kubernetes.io/arch` mapping in part (1) works against real labels, and the x86/aarch64 split falls exactly along the CPU/GPU pool boundary.

**The scale-group label is scoped as described** — nodes carry `iris-cw-use08a-scale-group` ∈ {`gb200`, `cpu-erapids`}, not `iris.pool`. Deriving the map from `label_prefix` resolves against these.

---

One conflict worth folding into part (2) before it ships.

**Pinning the 08a Kueue CPU flavor to `cpu-erapids` would make current CPU production work unschedulable.** `rav.datakit-fuzzy-validation-current-focus-prod-v16` requests per pod roughly 80% of a GB200 node's allocatable CPU and 90% of its memory, and is running many such pods right now. A `cd-gp-i64-erapids` node has well under half the cores one of those pods asks for, so pinned to that pool the job would not fit on any node, at any replica count — and the pool as a whole is a small fraction of what the job currently consumes.

That sizing is not accidental: the request is shaped to nearly fill a GB200 node and is only satisfiable there. A cluster-global default that assumes accelerator-free work fits the CPU pool does not hold on 08a.

This is not an argument against part (2) — the safe-default intent is right, and part (1) is unaffected. But the default needs a fallback path (or an explicit opt-out) for accelerator-free pods too large for the pinned pool, otherwise the change converts today's GPU-stranding into a hard pend for a production job. Worth deciding which of those failure modes is preferred, explicitly.

For context on the stranding half: that job's placement currently holds a large set of GB200 nodes at zero GPUs used, putting most of the cluster's idle GPUs out of reach. Filed as #8247 — it's a placement/packing gap rather than a pool-selection one, but the two interact directly, since a working `pool`/`arch` selector plus adequate CPU capacity would be the cleanest fix for both.
